# The Political Economy of Thin Work

## 1. Why markets tend to prefer thinner jobs

Firms generally optimize for things like:
- cost
- predictability
- speed
- legal defensibility
- scalability
- replaceability
- quality control
- throughput

And from that perspective, a worker with lots of discretion is often inconvenient.

Why?

Because discretion introduces:
- variance
- slowness
- conflict
- training costs
- harder evaluation
- more bargaining power
- more institutional dependence on specific persons

By contrast, thinner jobs are attractive because they are:
- easier to monitor
- easier to standardize
- easier to outsource
- easier to staff
- easier to automate incrementally
- easier to plug into software systems

AI intensifies this tendency because it makes it newly possible to decompose skilled roles into:
- recommendation systems
- scripted interactions
- exception handling
- dashboard monitoring
- compliance workflows
- style-adjustment layers

That means the market reward often goes not to preserving full human roles, but to **unbundling them into cheaper controllable pieces**.

---

## 2. The core economic temptation: de-skill the role, keep the output

This may be the master pattern.

A firm looks at a role and asks:
- Which parts require expensive human judgment?
- Which parts can be systematized?
- Which parts can be handed to lower-paid workers with AI support?
- Which parts can be monitored through metrics?
- Which parts only need the appearance of expertise?

Then the role gets redesigned.

Not necessarily eliminated.
Often **thinned**.

For example:
- not doctor replaced, but doctor increasingly constrained by system recommendations
- not teacher replaced, but teacher turned into platform manager
- not writer replaced, but writer shifted into brand-tone editing
- not analyst replaced, but analyst reduced to summarizing machine outputs
- not manager replaced, but manager narrowed into performance compliance and escalation

In each case, the output may remain acceptable or even improve.
But the role loses:
- developmental depth
- apprenticeship value
- scope of judgment
- ownership of standards

This is efficient in the narrow sense.
It may be disastrous in the civilizational sense.

---

## 3. Firms don’t capture the full value of human formation

This is crucial.

A company may rationally choose a workflow that produces:
- cheaper labor
- faster outputs
- tighter control
- lower training costs

even if that workflow contributes to a society with:
- weaker judgment
- fewer apprenticeships
- lower adult agency
- more dependence
- narrower pathways into expertise

Why? Because those wider losses are **externalities**.

The firm captures the gains.
Society absorbs the losses.

That is classic political economy.

Just as firms may underinvest in:
- clean air,
- public trust,
- worker health,
- civic stability,

they may also underinvest in the social reproduction of responsible human agency.

This is one of the most important points in the whole discussion:

> **Human formation is a public good, but thin work can be privately profitable.**

That creates structural pressure toward erosion unless something counterbalances it.

---

## 4. AI amplifies principal-agent logic

Organizations already struggle with trust.

Managers worry:
- Is the employee doing the work?
- Is quality consistent?
- Can I scale this without depending on exceptional individuals?
- Can I reduce error and liability?

AI appears as a solution because it promises:
- standardization
- recommendation consistency
- audit trails
- performance visibility
- lower reliance on tacit skill
- easier worker substitution

So from inside the organization, AI often looks less like “replace the human” and more like:
> “reduce the space in which unpredictable human judgment operates.”

That can be rational from a managerial standpoint.

But when generalized across an economy, it tends to produce:
- less craft
- less discretion
- less tacit development
- more procedural dependence
- more ceremonial accountability

So the market doesn’t need to hate workers to thin them.
It only needs to prefer control.

---

## 5. The measurement problem pushes toward simulation

Modern institutions reward what they can measure.

What can firms measure easily?
- response time
- volume
- customer ratings
- compliance rates
- output count
- turnaround speed
- engagement
- consistency

What is harder to measure?
- judgment
- trustworthiness
- long-horizon responsibility
- moral seriousness
- deep mentorship
- situational wisdom
- real authorship
- quality of interpretation

So firms often drift toward proxies.

AI deepens this because it improves performance on many measurable outputs.
That means organizations may increasingly reward:
- surface fluency
- responsiveness
- optimization against dashboards
- reliable presentation

while underrewarding what remains humanly precious but less legible.

This is how a system can become more efficient and less serious at the same time.

---

## 6. Consumers often reward convenience over depth

It’s not just firms.
Consumers are part of the political economy too.

Many people prefer:
- lower prices
- quicker service
- always-available support
- smoother interfaces
- personalized guidance
- less waiting
- “good enough” quality delivered instantly

That creates demand for systems that:
- reduce labor costs
- streamline interaction
- standardize service
- automate relational work
- make expertise feel ambient

In many domains, consumers won’t pay extra for:
- stronger apprenticeship pipelines
- deeper worker discretion
- locally rooted accountability
- process integrity
- human development in the abstract

So the market pressure is double:
- firms want controllability
- consumers want convenience

The result is a strong economic current toward thinner work.

Again: no villain needed.

---

## 7. Labor markets also encourage worker consent to thinning

Workers themselves may accept or even welcome thinner roles, at least in the short run.

Why?
Because thinner work can offer:
- easier entry
- less pressure
- more support
- lower skill thresholds
- reduced cognitive load
- less exposure to failure
- more immediate productivity

That makes sense, especially in stressed societies.

If many workers are:
- exhausted
- debt-burdened
- undertrained
- precarious
- juggling multiple demands

then AI-supported simplification can feel merciful.

And often it is, locally.

The difficulty is that what feels like relief in the short term may reduce:
- bargaining power
- skill accumulation
- autonomy
- pathways to mastery
- long-term dignity

So labor can become complicit in deskilling not because workers don’t value agency, but because they need survivable lives now.

That’s politically important.

You cannot defend thick work only by preaching virtue to tired people.

---

## 8. Shareholder and competition pressures reward short time horizons

Even firms that care about craft and worker development face competitive pressure.

If one company preserves:
- slower apprenticeship
- more human discretion
- employee development
- thicker roles

while another embraces:
- automated workflows
- metric-driven oversight
- lower training costs
- AI-mediated standardization

the second may outcompete the first on price or scale.

Then even well-intentioned leaders get pushed toward thinning.

This is why “ethical leadership” is not enough.
The issue is structural.

When markets reward extraction of value from roles without paying for the reproduction of the capacities behind those roles, underinvestment in human formation becomes normal.

A society can then slowly consume its stock of competence.

---

## 9. Professional institutions are one of the few counterweights

This is why professions matter.

Strong professions can resist pure market logic by insisting on:
- training standards
- apprenticeships
- licensing
- fiduciary duty
- ethical codes
- human accountability
- discretion protected from pure managerial override

They can say:
- medicine is not just throughput
- law is not just document production
- teaching is not just content delivery
- engineering is not just output optimization

In other words, professions can preserve roles against total decomposition into tasks.

But this requires professional self-confidence and public legitimacy.
And both have been weakening in many sectors.

If professions become fully subordinate to platform logic or managerial metrics, one major defense against thin work disappears.

---

## 10. Labor law usually protects wages and safety more than agency

This is a big gap.

Traditional labor politics often focuses on:
- pay
- hours
- benefits
- safety
- discrimination
- termination
- collective bargaining

All important.

But AI raises another issue:
## the structure of work itself

Questions like:
- Does the worker exercise real discretion?
- Is monitoring so tight that initiative disappears?
- Are workers accountable for systems they don’t control?
- Is there a path to skill growth?
- Has the role been deskilled through automation?
- Are apprenticeships being destroyed?

Current labor institutions are not very good at regulating these dimensions.

So even a workplace that is legal and moderately well-paid may still be profoundly thinning.

That means a humane AI politics may need to expand from labor protection to **labor constitution**:
not only what workers receive,
but what kinds of workers jobs are shaping them into.

---

## 11. Public institutions often copy the same mistakes

One might hope the state would balance the market.

Sometimes it can.
But public institutions also love:
- metrics
- standardization
- compliance systems
- cost reduction
- risk management
- auditability

So schools, hospitals, agencies, and public services may also adopt AI in ways that:
- narrow human discretion
- increase surveillance
- proceduralize judgment
- preserve nominal accountability while centralizing real control

In other words, bureaucracy and markets can converge.

This matters because it means the alternative to thin private work is not automatically thick public work.

Both sectors can drift toward managed cognition.

---

## 12. Why class becomes the predictable outcome

Now we can see why class is such a danger.

If the broad economy trends toward thinner roles, then those with resources will disproportionately secure:
- professions with retained discretion
- firms that still value craft
- networks that offer apprenticeship
- leadership paths with real judgment
- low-surveillance autonomy
- opportunities to compound responsibility

Others will be sorted into:
- heavily structured roles
- lower-discretion service work
- platform dependence
- metric management
- machine-mediated supervision
- pseudo-responsibility without real control

So inequality becomes not merely:
- who has more money

but:
- who gets to keep becoming a person through work

This is a much more destabilizing divide.

Because if one class still develops:
- judgment
- courage
- discretion
- public voice
- authority under uncertainty

while another is habituated to management systems,
then hierarchy begins to feel naturalized.

That is a political disaster for democracy.

---

# So what would a better political economy look like?

Not anti-market in some total sense.
Not anti-technology.
But intentionally structured to resist the worst thinning pressures.

I’d break it into six areas.

---

## 13. First: regulate for real human accountability

In high-stakes domains, law should insist that if a human is accountable, the human must also have:
- real discretion
- real visibility into the basis of decisions
- authority to override
- time and support to exercise judgment

Otherwise “human in the loop” is a fiction.

This applies in areas like:
- healthcare
- law
- education
- finance
- public administration
- safety-critical engineering

A worker should not be legally or morally blamed for a decision they are structurally prevented from shaping.

---

## 14. Second: protect apprenticeship pipelines

Society may need explicit policy to preserve developmental ladders in professions.

That could include:
- requirements for supervised human practice
- limits on full automation of training-stage tasks
- incentives for apprentice hiring
- accreditation standards that include direct performance
- public funding for craft and technical formation
- professional rules about what novices must still learn firsthand

This is not nostalgia.
It is reproduction of expertise.

If AI erases the path by which juniors become seniors, the profession cannibalizes its future.

---

## 15. Third: redesign productivity metrics

Organizations need better measures than:
- speed
- quantity
- customer sentiment
- dashboard compliance

They should also value:
- sound judgment
- quality of interpretation
- mentorship
- error detection
- trustworthiness
- long-term problem solving
- contribution to team capability

Harder to measure, yes.
But if only the easy metrics count, jobs will be built around what machines and managed workflows already optimize best.

Political economy is partly a measurement regime.

What gets measured gets organized.
What gets organized shapes persons.

---

## 16. Fourth: strengthen professional and worker voice in tech deployment

AI adoption should not be only a management or vendor decision.

Workers and professions should have a say in:
- what gets automated
- what remains human work
- how accountability is assigned
- what training is preserved
- what kinds of surveillance are acceptable
- whether a system assists or de-skills

This could happen through:
- unions
- works councils
- professional bodies
- licensing boards
- co-determination structures
- public-sector governance rules

Without institutional voice, AI deployment will predictably optimize for managerial control.

---

## 17. Fifth: support non-work institutions of adulthood

If the economy cannot fully preserve thick work for everyone, then society must strengthen other sites of responsibility:
- family-support policy
- civic service
- community organizations
- religious and voluntary associations
- public arts and amateur culture
- local governance participation
- sports and outdoor programs
- adult education and craft institutions

This is easy to dismiss as secondary.
It is not.

If work thins and all other formative institutions are also weak, then adult agency has nowhere to live.

That is how a society becomes comfortable and childlike at once.

---

## 18. Sixth: accept that some friction is a public good

This may be the strangest but most important point.

A market economy generally treats friction as waste.
Often that’s right.

But some friction preserves:
- skill formation
- discretion
- responsibility
- judgment
- trust

So a decent political economy may need to defend certain forms of “inefficiency” because they are actually developmental infrastructure.

Examples:
- slower training pathways
- in-person mentoring
- human review with true authority
- longer apprenticeship
- live deliberation
- local institutional redundancy
- non-optimized care roles

These may look inefficient on a dashboard.
They may be essential in a civilization.

---

# The real political question

All of this leads to a harder conclusion:

## the AI economy will not naturally converge on the humanly best arrangement

It will more likely converge on a mix of:
- convenience
- control
- standardization
- deskilling
- pseudo-accountability
- selective islands of high-agency work for the advantaged

unless laws, norms, professions, and institutions push back.

So the debate is not:
- innovation vs stagnation

It is:
- what kind of human beings an economy is allowed to assume, reward, and reproduce

That is a political question in the deepest sense.

---

# My blunt synthesis

If we leave this mostly to market incentives, I expect:

- firms will thin many roles into AI-assisted workflows
- workers will be retained formally but narrowed substantively
- consumers will reward convenience
- apprenticeship will erode in many fields
- responsibility-rich work will become more concentrated
- education will struggle to justify thick formation
- class inequality will increasingly become agency inequality

That is the default trajectory.

The better path requires intervention—not necessarily heavy-handed central planning, but real institutional counterweights.

---

# Compressed version

## Why markets drift toward thin work
Because thin work is often:
- cheaper
- more controllable
- more measurable
- more scalable
- less dependent on hard-to-replace human judgment

## Why that’s a social problem
Because the losses:
- reduced agency
- weaker apprenticeship
- thinner adulthood
- diminished democracy

are not borne fully by the firms making the decisions.

## What must counteract it
- law
- professional norms
- worker voice
- institutional design
- public investment in formative roles and communities

---

## Final line

A society that wants adults cannot treat the structure of work as a morally neutral byproduct of efficiency.

It has to ask, deliberately:

> **What kinds of roles are we creating, what capacities do they require, and who still gets to become a person through them?**

If you want, the next best move is one of these:

1. **Design principles for dignity-bearing work** — a practical manifesto for employers, professions, and policymakers  
2. **A case study profession** — e.g. medicine, teaching, law, software, management  
3. **A political argument** — whether liberal societies can justify protecting agency as a public good without becoming perfectionist

My vote: **case study profession**. That’s where abstractions get tested.

# Case Study Profession: Teaching in an AI Age

## The central question

> Will AI help teachers do more truly human teaching, or will it redesign teaching into the management of machine-mediated instruction?

That is the hinge.

Because teaching is not just:
- explaining content
- grading assignments
- assigning practice
- tracking standards

Teaching is also:
- noticing misunderstanding
- designing difficulty
- establishing norms
- calling students into seriousness
- reading motivation and avoidance
- judging when to push and when to support
- creating a shared intellectual culture
- forming attention, speech, and responsibility

If AI automates the first cluster well, that could be liberating.

If institutions then conclude the second cluster is optional, that would be a disaster.

---

# 1. What makes teaching a “thick” profession

Teaching, at its best, is a responsibility-rich role because it involves all of the following:

## A. Judgment under uncertainty
Teachers constantly decide:
- whether a student is confused or disengaged
- whether a class is ready to move on
- whether an answer reflects thought or bluffing
- whether to correct, probe, wait, redirect, or challenge
- how hard to make the next task

These are not merely technical decisions.
They are situational judgments.

## B. Relational authority
A good teacher must establish a form of authority that is:
- real but not domineering
- demanding but not humiliating
- personal but not indulgent

That is very hard to standardize.

## C. Interpretation of persons
Teachers are continually interpreting:
- effort
- fear
- talent
- resistance
- social dynamics
- confidence
- growth

Not perfectly, of course. But the role depends on seeing more than outputs.

## D. Long-horizon responsibility
Teachers are not just producing today’s answers.
They are shaping:
- habits of mind
- self-conception
- standards
- relationship to difficulty
- moral tone of a classroom

That makes teaching formative, not just instructional.

This is why teaching is a good case study.  
If even teaching gets thinned into content management, the broader pattern is clear.

---

# 2. How AI could genuinely help teachers

There are many good uses, and they matter.

AI could reduce burdens that often crowd out the best parts of teaching:

- first-pass grading on low-stakes exercises
- generating practice sets at different levels
- creating feedback templates
- translating materials for multilingual students
- helping draft quizzes or rubrics
- summarizing curriculum resources
- suggesting intervention ideas
- supporting accessibility accommodations
- reducing repetitive admin and documentation
- identifying patterns in student errors

Used well, this could free teachers for more of the work only they can do:
- conferencing
- oral feedback
- discussion
- live diagnosis
- classroom culture
- relationship-building
- formative questioning

In this version, AI removes **clerical drag** and strengthens professional discretion.

That is the hopeful path.

---

# 3. How AI could thin teaching instead

Here is the darker version.

A school system under budget and staffing pressure sees AI and says:

- it can explain lessons
- it can generate personalized exercises
- it can give immediate feedback
- it can track mastery
- it can suggest interventions
- it can draft parent emails
- it can monitor progress
- it can standardize instruction

From there, the teacher’s role gets redefined.

The teacher becomes less:
- intellectual guide
- moral authority
- interpreter of classroom life
- designer of formative struggle

and more:
- behavior manager
- software troubleshooter
- dashboard monitor
- compliance intermediary
- emotional support layer around machine-directed instruction

This is teaching preserved in title but thinned in substance.

It may even look efficient:
- more individualized pacing
- more data
- more consistency
- lower training burden for new hires
- easier substitution of less experienced staff

But the role loses:
- judgment
- authorship
- craft
- real pedagogical discretion

And once that happens, the profession becomes less attractive to serious people, less capable of reproducing excellence, and easier to control bureaucratically.

---

# 4. The political economy of thinning teachers

Teaching is especially vulnerable because education systems are often under pressure for:

- cost control
- standardized outcomes
- legal defensibility
- measurable performance
- staff replaceability
- quick onboarding
- reduced dependence on unusually strong teachers

From an administrative perspective, AI can look like a way to:
- smooth teacher quality variation
- reduce planning time
- make curricula more uniform
- decrease reliance on highly skilled professionals
- gather more data for accountability systems

That is understandable.

But the danger is that the system starts treating teacher judgment as a source of inconsistency rather than the core of the profession.

Once that happens, “improvement” means:
- tighter scripts
- more centralized tools
- more analytics
- less local discretion
- more intervention according to software signals

In short: a thinner teacher in a more technologically saturated system.

---

# 5. The key distinction: instruction delivery vs formation

This is where the profession must defend itself conceptually.

If teaching is defined mainly as **content delivery**, then AI will inevitably look like a substitute.

If teaching is defined as **formation through instructional, relational, and judgment-bearing practice**, then AI looks more like a subordinate tool.

That is not a semantic difference.  
It determines institutional design.

Because if the real job is:
- “make sure each student receives explanations and practice,”

then software can plausibly do much of it.

But if the real job is:
- “form students in attention, understanding, speech, accountability, and response to difficulty,”

then teaching remains deeply human, even when tools are involved.

This means the future of teaching depends partly on whether the profession can state clearly what it is for.

---

# 6. What thick teaching would preserve

A dignity-bearing teacher role in an AI age should still include at least these elements:

## A. Authority over formative design
Teachers should decide where students must struggle directly, where support is useful, and what counts as learning.

## B. Interpretation of student understanding
Not just data consumption, but real judgment:
- Can this student explain it?
- Is this confusion conceptual or motivational?
- Is this draft owned or borrowed?
- What kind of next challenge is right?

## C. Classroom culture building
A healthy classroom is not just individualized software use in parallel.
It is a moral and intellectual community.

## D. Live discourse
Teachers should still lead:
- seminars
- questioning
- oral checks
- discussions
- debates
- public explanation

## E. Mentorship and consequence-bearing judgment
Teachers must still be able to say:
- this work is not yet honest
- this effort is insufficient
- this student needs challenge, not rescue
- this class can go deeper
- this norm matters

Without that, they are not really teachers.

---

# 7. What thin teaching looks like in practice

A thinned teacher role would probably include more of the following:

- centrally generated lesson sequences
- AI-created feedback replacing teacher comments
- personalization engines assigning work by algorithm
- student-facing tutors doing much of the explaining
- teachers spending class time troubleshooting and managing behavior
- dashboards telling teachers who is “off track”
- pressure to trust platform outputs over professional intuition
- scripted interventions generated by software
- less direct engagement with student thinking
- less need for deep subject mastery

The teacher remains present, but increasingly as a **facilitator of a system**.

This may still involve care. It may still involve effort.  
But it involves less real professional authorship.

And over time, that changes who enters the profession and what kind of person it forms.

---

# 8. Why this matters beyond schools

Because teaching is also how a society reproduces citizens.

If teachers lose:
- authority
- discretion
- intellectual centrality
- professional pride

then schools may still function administratively while becoming weaker at producing:
- judgment
- seriousness
- common standards
- democratic habits
- resistance to simulation

In other words, thinning teachers also thins the next generation.

That’s why this case study matters beyond the profession itself.

---

# 9. What better AI deployment in teaching would look like

A serious model would follow a simple rule:

> Use AI to reduce clerical and bureaucratic burden so that teachers can spend more time on live judgment, culture, and student thinking.

Concretely:

## Good deployment
- summarize mundane admin
- generate optional practice
- support translation/accessibility
- help teachers draft but not replace comments
- identify patterns for teacher review
- provide planning support
- assist with low-stakes retrieval practice
- automate repetitive formatting and paperwork

## Bad deployment
- replace direct feedback on important work
- substitute software tutoring for teacher instruction by default
- centralize lesson design so tightly that teacher judgment shrinks
- use analytics to overrule local understanding
- turn classrooms into individualized screen environments
- evaluate teachers mainly by machine-measured outputs
- weaken subject expertise requirements because tools can “fill gaps”

The difference is whether AI creates more room for teaching or less need for teachers.

---

# 10. The apprenticeship issue inside teaching

This is a huge one.

How do new teachers become good?

Usually through:
- observing experienced teachers
- trying lessons
- failing visibly
- learning to read a room
- adjusting in real time
- designing questions
- grading lots of imperfect work
- discovering what students actually misunderstand
- building authority through repetition

If AI systems take over too many of these intermediate burdens, novice teachers may become more manageable but less formed.

For example:
- if lesson plans are always generated,
- if feedback is mostly automated,
- if software handles pacing,
- if intervention prompts are system-generated,

then the novice may never develop strong pedagogical judgment.

They will perform the outer role without building the inner craft.

This is the same developmental paradox we saw in other professions:
automation can remove the very experiences through which competence grows.

So preserving teaching quality over time requires preserving teacher formation, not just student outcomes.

---

# 11. The class danger in teaching

This is perhaps the starkest political dimension.

If elite schools use AI to free strong teachers for:
- seminars
- writing conferences
- oral exams
- mentorship
- rich projects

while mass-market schools use AI to:
- substitute for scarce teachers
- scale larger classes
- automate feedback
- manage behavior and remediation cheaply

then inequality becomes self-reinforcing.

The privileged get more human judgment.
The rest get more machine mediation.

That means:
- one class is taught by adults with authority
- another is increasingly processed through systems

Nothing could be more socially consequential.

Because then the very students who most need serious adult formation are given the thinnest version of schooling.

That would be the educational form of the two-civilizations future.

---

# 12. What policy should protect in teaching

If we wanted to keep teaching a dignity-bearing profession, policy would need to protect a few non-negotiables.

## A. Preserve teacher authority over core assessment
Especially for high-stakes work:
- writing
- oral performance
- interpretation
- class participation
- serious projects

## B. Limit fully automated substitution in core instructional domains
AI can assist, but student formation should not be outsourced to constant machine mediation.

## C. Fund teacher time
Without time, teachers will be forced into thin-tech convenience whether they want it or not.

This means:
- planning time
- feedback time
- professional collaboration
- manageable class sizes where possible

## D. Protect apprenticeship and teacher development
New teachers need:
- modeling
- coaching
- live practice
- observation
- subject-specific formation

## E. Resist evaluation regimes based only on easy metrics
If teachers are judged only by scores, completion, and dashboards, the role will thin fast.

Those protections are not anti-innovation.
They are protections for the integrity of the profession.

---

# 13. The liberal defense of teaching as a thick profession

There’s a broader political point here too.

A liberal society should care about keeping teaching thick not because it wants to impose one doctrine of the good life, but because teaching helps preserve capacities necessary for freedom itself:

- judgment
- speech
- attention
- shared standards
- civic reasoning
- non-dependence on systems
- the ability to encounter persons rather than merely interfaces

That gives a public justification for protecting the profession.

You do not need a perfectionist state to argue that children should be educated by adults whose role still includes serious human judgment.

That is a freedom-protecting claim.

---

# 14. The bleak scenario for teaching

If the bad equilibrium wins, teaching becomes:

- lower-status
- more monitored
- more standardized
- less intellectually central
- increasingly software-mediated
- less attractive to capable adults
- split by class between elite human-rich schools and system-heavy mass schooling

In that world, “AI for education” will really mean:
**better formed adults for the privileged, manageable instructional support for everyone else.**

That is a grim but plausible outcome.

---

# 15. The hopeful scenario for teaching

In the better version:

- AI takes over bureaucratic drag
- teachers spend more time in discussion, feedback, and mentorship
- assessment shifts toward ownership and live understanding
- teacher expertise becomes more valuable, not less
- schools protect no-AI and AI-with-judgment zones
- professional norms clarify where human educational authority must remain
- students get both excellent tools and real teachers

That would make teaching more intellectually serious and more human at once.

It is possible — but it requires design and defense.

---

# 16. Compressed conclusion

Teaching is a revealing case because it forces the central distinction:

> **Will AI help professionals exercise deeper human judgment, or will it narrow them into supervisors of machine-shaped process?**

If the former, the profession thickens.
If the latter, it hollows.

And because teaching forms the next generation, this is not just a labor issue.  
It is a constitutional issue for the culture.

---

- pluralism is real
- power corrupts
- states are bad at enforcing virtue
- citizens disagree deeply about meaning

So if someone says,
> “The state should preserve struggle because struggle builds character,”

a liberal will reasonably ask:
- Which struggle?
- According to whose values?
- Why should the state decide?
- Isn’t this just moral imposition?

That objection has force.

But I think our argument does **not** need to rest on a thick perfectionist account of the good life.

It can rest on something narrower and more politically defensible:

> a free society has reason to preserve the human capacities without which freedom becomes hollow, manipulable, or merely formal.

That is a different claim.

---

# 1. The distinction between neutrality about ends and neutrality about capacities

A liberal society may try to remain relatively open about final ends:
- art or family
- faith or secularism
- ambition or contemplation
- entrepreneurship or public service
- city life or rural life

But it cannot be neutral about the basic capacities citizens need in order to pursue any of those ends meaningfully.

Those capacities include things like:
- attention
- literacy
- judgment
- self-command
- ability to weigh reasons
- tolerance for uncertainty
- resistance to manipulation
- capacity for commitment
- ability to participate in shared institutions
- ability to bear some responsibility for one’s actions

These are not one sect’s vision of sainthood.
They are closer to the **civic and psychological infrastructure of freedom**.

So the state need not say:
> “You must become a heroic, deeply authentic person.”

It may legitimately say:
> “We have a public interest in citizens not being systematically deskilled, manipulated, infantilized, or rendered dependent in ways that undermine meaningful self-government.”

That is a liberal argument, not an anti-liberal one.

---

# 2. Why liberalism already depends on thicker human assumptions than it admits

Modern liberal societies often talk as if all they need to protect is:
- rights
- consent
- opportunity
- non-coercion

But in practice, those things only work well if citizens have some degree of:
- judgment
- self-restraint
- reality contact
- ability to deliberate
- ability to resist flattery and fear
- ability to act without constant external scripting

In other words, liberal order quietly presupposes a certain kind of person.

Not a saint.
Not a philosopher-king.
But not a fully managed, convenience-maximized dependent either.

That means there is a tension inside liberalism:

## liberalism often denies the need to shape persons,
## while depending on persons who have already been shaped.

That shaping used to come more from:
- family
- religion
- civic culture
- local institutions
- slower forms of work
- educational norms

But if AI-heavy systems erode those formation-structures, liberalism may find that the kind of citizen it assumes is no longer reproduced automatically.

Then it has to choose:
- either defend the conditions of agency more explicitly,
- or drift into a society of formally free but substantively guided individuals.

That’s the deeper stakes.

---

# 3. The strongest liberal justification: anti-domination

If I had to ground the whole case in one political principle, it would be:

## anti-domination

A society should worry not only about direct coercion, but about conditions in which people become easy to steer, govern, manipulate, or administratively manage.

That is a very old republican insight, but it fits here perfectly.

If citizens increasingly:
- outsource judgment,
- lose competence,
- rely on opaque systems,
- prefer simulations of participation,
- cannot function without machine guidance,

then even if they retain formal rights, they become more governable in a deep sense.

They are easier to:
- nudge
- pacify
- target
- administrate
- replace symbolically
- include procedurally while excluding substantively

That is a real threat to freedom.

So preserving thick capacities is justified not because the state wants to impose “meaning,” but because citizens who cannot judge, attend, and act with some independence are more vulnerable to domination by:
- firms
- platforms
- bureaucracies
- political actors
- algorithmic systems

This turns our earlier argument into a recognizably liberal one:
not moral heroism for its own sake,
but **protection against becoming governable in the wrong way**.

---

# 4. Why this is not just paternalism in disguise

A critic might still say:
“Fine words, but isn’t this just paternalism with better branding?”

Sometimes it could become that.
But it doesn’t have to.

The distinction is this:

## paternalism says:
we know what is good for you, so we will steer you toward the better life

## the freedom-preserving version says:
certain conditions systematically erode the capacities needed for self-government, and society may resist that erosion

That’s narrower.

For example, the state need not decide:
- whether you should become an artist or engineer
- whether religion or secular life is better
- whether you should seek contemplation or ambition

But it may have reason to care whether institutions are making people:
- less able to think independently
- less able to endure difficulty
- less able to distinguish reality from simulation
- less able to participate in shared self-rule
- more dependent on systems they cannot question

That is less like commanding virtue and more like preserving the **minimum thickness of the free person**.

---

# 5. Education is the clearest case

This is why schools are politically easier to defend than, say, regulating adult leisure.

Children are not fully formed choosers.
Education is always formative.
And democratic societies already accept that schools should cultivate:
- literacy
- numeracy
- civic understanding
- habits of attention
- truthfulness
- cooperation
- some capacity for self-discipline

So when we say schools should preserve:
- direct thinking
- authorship
- oral defense
- responsibility for one’s work
- resistance to passive tool dependence

we are not introducing a bizarre perfectionist doctrine.

We are specifying what meaningful education requires under new technological conditions.

That is highly defensible in liberal terms.

The harder question comes later, with adults and work.

---

# 6. Work is harder, but still not morally neutral

A liberal state should be cautious about dictating the meaning of work.
But it is not required to treat all labor structures as equally acceptable.

We already regulate work because it affects:
- dignity
- power
- health
- coercion
- dependence
- vulnerability

So extending that concern to forms of work that systematically:
- deskill,
- displace judgment,
- create pseudo-accountability,
- heighten domination through surveillance,
- or erode pathways to competence

is not some radical departure.

It is a recognition that labor markets shape the kind of people citizens become and the kind of power relations they inhabit.

A free society may reasonably say:
- workers should not be reduced to accountability without control
- professions should preserve real discretion where responsibility is assigned
- apprenticeship matters
- systems should not make human judgment purely ceremonial

That is still about freedom, not about mandating spiritual depth.

---

# 7. The liberal danger on the other side: thin proceduralism

I think the real threat is that liberal societies may retreat into a very thin procedural language:
- informed choice
- access
- transparency
- consent
- personalization
- user control

All of that matters.

But it can become misleading if people are choosing within environments engineered to:
- remove friction
- substitute simulation
- guide behavior
- reward passivity
- reduce practice in self-command

Then “choice” may remain, but the chooser weakens.

And once the chooser weakens enough, procedural liberalism becomes unstable.
It starts to depend more and more on:
- technocratic administration
- paternalistic system design
- behavior shaping from above
- ever more assistance to cope with the consequences of dependence

This is the paradox:
if liberalism refuses to defend the formative conditions of agency, it may end up governing weaker agents more intrusively.

So a society that wants less domination in the long run may need more courage in defending formative institutions in the short run.

---

# 8. The legitimate scope of public action

So what can a liberal society justifiably do?

I think it can do quite a lot, as long as it stays within the right frame.

## It can:
- shape schools around ownership, judgment, and shared standards
- regulate manipulative AI systems, especially for children
- require human accountability to be real where it is formally assigned
- protect apprenticeship and professional discretion
- support institutions of civic and communal life
- limit exploitative simulation in care, education, and political communication
- prevent concentration of formative goods only among elites

## It should be more cautious about:
- policing adult private choices simply for being shallow
- banning harmless convenience because it seems spiritually inferior
- imposing one official doctrine of authenticity
- treating all assistance as decadence
- criminalizing adult preference for easier forms of life

That line seems important.

The public aim should be:
> protect the ecology of agency

not:
> coerce existential nobility

---

# 9. The strongest objection: who decides what counts as “thick”?

This remains the hardest objection.

People disagree.
Some overvalue discipline.
Some romanticize hardship.
Some have class-coded ideas of seriousness.
Some stigmatize dependency too easily.

All true.

So any public defense of thicker roles and institutions must be:
- contestable
- pluralism-aware
- empirically informed
- open to revision
- careful about disability and inequality
- aware of how often “character” talk has been abused

That means we should justify protections in terms like:
- accountability
- non-domination
- developmental necessity
- equal access to formative institutions
- resistance to manipulation
- genuine capability

rather than in vague invocations of “real life” or “authenticity.”

Those latter terms can become smug very quickly.

---

# 10. A liberal formula

Here’s the most compact version I can offer:

> **A liberal society may legitimately protect the conditions of human agency when those conditions are prerequisites for meaningful freedom, equal citizenship, and resistance to domination.**

That gives a principled basis for:
- serious education
- dignity-bearing work
- limits on manipulative AI systems
- preserving human judgment in certain roles
- concern about simulation replacing social reality

without requiring the state to settle every question of ultimate meaning.

It is a modestly perfectionist liberalism, perhaps—but one ordered toward freedom’s prerequisites, not toward one official way of life.

---

# 11. The deeper truth: every regime forms people anyway

This may be the final point.

The fantasy of a neutral society is just that—a fantasy.

Every social order forms persons through:
- institutions
- incentives
- media
- labor structures
- technology
- status systems
- laws
- defaults

So the real question is never:
> Will society shape people?

It is:
> **What kinds of people will our systems tend to produce?**

If AI-heavy institutions tend to produce:
- more dependence
- less judgment
- lower frustration tolerance
- more managed passivity
- weaker civic capacity

then refusing to respond in the name of neutrality is not principled restraint.

It is choosing one form of formation while pretending not to choose at all.

That is why I think liberal societies can and should act here.

Not to impose greatness.
Not to sanctify struggle.
But to ensure that freedom does not become merely the permission to live in well-administered dependence.

---

# My answer, plainly

## Can liberal societies justify protecting thick roles without imposing a controversial ideal of the good life?

**Yes.**

They can do so by arguing that:
- meaningful freedom requires agency, not just options
- democracy requires citizens capable of judgment
- anti-domination requires limits on dependency-inducing systems
- children deserve formation, not just support
- accountability must not be detached from control
- class inequality in access to formative institutions is politically corrosive

That is enough to justify a lot.

Not everything.
But a lot.

---

# One-sentence version

**The best liberal defense of “thick” institutions is not that they make people noble, but that they preserve the human capacities without which freedom, citizenship, and non-domination become increasingly hollow.**

If you want, there are two excellent next moves:

1. **Write the public philosophy version** — a concise essay or speech arguing this position to a democratic audience  
2. **Write the opposing case** — the strongest liberal argument against this whole view, so we can test whether it really holds up

- human judgment
- truthfulness
- shared standards
- resistance to passive dependence

- rely heavily on tools
- pursue entertainment
- prefer guided environments

- courts and law
- medicine
- child development
- public administration
- high-trust professions

- equal standing
- non-domination
- public trust
- reproduction of agency across generations

- entertainment
- hobby use
- low-stakes self-expression
- adult companionship choices
- convenience consumption

Those things matter. But they are not enough.

Freedom also depends on certain human capacities:
- the ability to pay attention
- the ability to judge
- the ability to understand reasons
- the ability to resist manipulation
- the ability to act without being guided at every step
- the ability to take responsibility for what one says and does

- surveillance
- concentration of power

then something important begins to thin out.

Through a thousand small reliefs.

The right goal is not to preserve hardship for its own sake.

A lot of effort is pointless and degrading:
- repetitive bureaucracy
- dangerous labor
- exhausting administrative nonsense
- performative busywork
- rote tasks that consume life without deepening it

- writing in one’s own words
- solving a problem before seeing the answer
- caring for another person
- making a judgment under uncertainty

- economic incentives
- laws and defaults

- speed over reflection
- convenience over competence
- dependence over judgment
- simulation over substance

- speak and defend a claim

- oral defense
- close reading
- live problem-solving
- attributable collaboration
- serious teacher judgment

That is not just unfair.

- ensure that the formative parts of life do not become luxury goods

The real question is whether we will use it to make human beings more capable, or whether we will gradually build a society in which fewer and fewer people are asked to exercise judgment, bear responsibility, and become fully adult.

We should want more access.  
We should want technology that genuinely helps.

But we should not design a world in which convenience steadily replaces the very experiences through which human beings become fit for freedom.

Because a society of well-assisted dependents may be comfortable.  
It may even be affluent.  
But it will not be fully free.

**The task is not to reject technology. It is to build institutions that use technology without surrendering the human capacities on which freedom, citizenship, and dignity depend.**

This is not an argument for glorifying hardship. Much effort really is pointless and degrading: repetitive paperwork, dangerous labor, administrative nonsense, the theater of busyness. We should gladly use technology to remove those burdens.

But not every difficulty is the same. Some effort is part of how people become capable. Learning to read carefully. Writing in your own words. Solving a problem before seeing the answer. Making a judgment under uncertainty. Building trust by carrying responsibility over time.

A healthy society should remove needless burdens without removing the kinds of challenge through which people grow into adulthood.

Some will object that this argument smuggles in a moral vision of the good life. Isn’t this just a high-minded way of telling people how to live?

That concern deserves a serious answer.

A liberal society should not impose one official ideal of human flourishing. It should not decide that every citizen must be spiritually deep, artistically serious, or highly self-disciplined.

But that is not the claim. The narrower claim is that a free society may protect the capacities people need in order to live as free and equal citizens. Literacy, judgment, accountability, and resistance to manipulation are not elite preferences. They are part of the infrastructure of freedom.

And no society is neutral about whether those capacities grow stronger or weaker. Schools shape them. Workplaces shape them. Media systems shape them. Technology platforms shape them. The question is never whether people will be formed. It is by what.

If we do nothing, we are not choosing neutrality. We are allowing commercial systems, bureaucratic systems, and optimization systems to do the shaping by default. And those systems often reward speed over reflection, convenience over competence, dependence over judgment, and simulation over substance.

That is not freedom untouched. It is freedom unguarded.

Schools are the clearest place to begin. They should not become places where students merely learn to produce acceptable outputs with powerful tools. They should remain places where students learn to read with attention, write with ownership, defend a claim, solve problems they do not yet know how to solve, and use tools without handing over their minds.

That means preserving in-class writing, oral defense, close reading, live problem-solving, serious teacher judgment, and other forms of learning that cannot be fully outsourced.

This is not anti-technology. It is pro-education.

But school is not enough. If young people are educated for judgment and responsibility, then sent into workplaces where they mostly approve machine outputs, follow dashboards, manage tone, and bear responsibility without real control, those capacities will fade.

So we should care not only about wages and efficiency, but about the structure of work itself. Do workers have real discretion? Do they develop skill over time? Are they accountable for decisions they can actually shape? Do professional roles still involve human judgment, or only ceremonial oversight?

An economy that makes responsibility thinner may still be productive. But it will not be neutral about the kind of citizens it produces.

Here the deepest danger comes into view. The conditions for becoming a serious, capable adult may themselves become a luxury good.

If wealthy families and elite institutions preserve demanding schools, mentorship, strong norms of ownership, and meaningful responsibility, while everyone else is increasingly routed through systems optimized for support, personalization, and manageable output, then inequality becomes more than economic.

It becomes inequality in agency.

One class keeps learning how to judge, decide, and lead. Another is increasingly guided, assisted, and managed. That is not just unfair. It is dangerous for democracy.

A free society does not need to regulate every private choice. It should not criminalize convenience or appoint itself supervisor of private meaning.

But it can do some basic things. It can protect serious education for all, not just the privileged. It can regulate manipulative AI systems, especially those aimed at children. It can require that formal accountability be matched by real human control. It can preserve apprenticeship and skill formation in work. And it can protect public institutions from collapsing into simulation and dashboard governance.

Why? For a simple reason: freedom requires more than permission. It requires people still capable of using freedom well enough not to be dominated.

AI can make life easier. We should welcome that.

But we should not build a society in which convenience steadily replaces the very experiences through which human beings become capable of freedom.

A society of well-assisted dependents may be comfortable. It may be efficient. It may even be affluent.

But it will not be fully free.

# AI, Freedom, and the Institutions That Make Self-Government Possible

Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly through schools, workplaces, and public institutions. It promises real gains: lower administrative burden, faster access to information, more personalized support, and new tools for learning and productivity.

Those benefits are significant and should be welcomed.

But policymakers should focus on more than adoption rates or efficiency gains. The deeper question is whether AI is being deployed in ways that strengthen human capability — or in ways that gradually reduce the exercise of judgment, responsibility, and skill.

That question matters because a free society depends on more than consumer choice or technical access. It also depends on citizens having the capacities needed for self-government: literacy, attention, judgment, accountability, and resistance to manipulation. If those capacities weaken, freedom may remain formally intact while becoming thinner in practice.

This is not an argument against innovation. It is an argument for institutional design.

The AI debate often centers on headline risks: misinformation, surveillance, labor displacement, and market concentration. Those concerns are real. But there is another challenge that deserves equal attention: the possibility that schools, workplaces, and public systems will increasingly offload the very tasks through which people develop competence and agency.

If students rely on AI before learning to think through a problem, if workers are held accountable for machine-shaped decisions they do not truly control, or if public institutions come to reward output quality while caring less about human understanding, then society may become more efficient while its citizens become less capable.

That is not a purely cultural concern. It is a governance concern.

## Schools are the first test

Education is the clearest starting point. In an AI-rich environment, schools will have to decide whether they are primarily in the business of helping students generate acceptable outputs — or of forming students who can understand, judge, and communicate with real ownership.

That requires preserving forms of learning that cannot be fully outsourced:
- in-class writing
- oral defense
- close reading
- live problem-solving
- attributable collaboration
- serious teacher evaluation

AI can be valuable in education when it supports practice, accessibility, feedback, and differentiated instruction. But if it begins to replace first-pass thinking, sustained reading, and direct demonstration of understanding, schools risk undermining the capacities they are supposed to build.

The policy implication is straightforward: public education systems should set clear standards for where AI assists learning and where students must still demonstrate independent understanding. The formative parts of education should not become luxury goods available only in elite settings.

## Work is the second test

The same issue appears in labor markets.

Much AI adoption today is framed in terms of task efficiency. But the more important unit is often the role, not the task. A healthy professional role includes discretion, accountability, skill development, and ownership over outcomes. If AI is used mainly to decompose such roles into narrower, easier-to-monitor functions, work may become more standardized but less dignity-bearing.

That matters not only for worker satisfaction, but for democratic resilience. Adults develop and sustain many of their civic capacities through roles that require judgment, reliability, and consequence-bearing responsibility. If those roles steadily erode, society may produce more formally employed people but fewer substantively self-governing adults.

This suggests a broader policy agenda than AI safety narrowly conceived. Policymakers and institutional leaders should ask:
- Does AI remove drudgery while preserving meaningful discretion?
- Are workers being held responsible for outputs they do not really control?
- Are apprenticeship pathways being weakened?
- Are professional standards being thinned in the name of efficiency?
- Are organizations preserving human judgment where accountability still rests with human beings?

These are labor-market and institutional-design questions, not just technical ones.

## The class risk is growing

Perhaps the most serious long-term concern is that the institutions which build capable adults may become increasingly stratified.

If affluent families and elite institutions preserve demanding schools, mentorship, strong writing and speaking norms, and responsibility-rich pathways into work, while mass systems rely more heavily on AI-mediated support, personalization, and automated guidance, inequality will deepen in a new way.

It will not be only inequality of income or credentials. It will become inequality of agency.

One group will continue to practice judgment, authorship, and leadership. Another will become increasingly accustomed to guidance, assistance, and managed performance. A democracy can tolerate many forms of inequality, but sustained inequality in the development of civic and practical agency is especially corrosive.

That is why this issue should be treated not only as a matter of innovation policy, but as a matter of equal citizenship.

## A targeted public agenda

A liberal society does not need to police every private choice or treat convenience as a moral failing. But it can take practical steps to protect the institutional foundations of self-government.

A serious agenda would include:
- protecting rigorous, human-led education in public systems
- setting standards for AI use in schools that preserve direct demonstration of understanding
- regulating manipulative AI systems aimed at children and adolescents
- requiring that formal accountability in high-stakes roles be matched by real human control
- preserving apprenticeship and skill formation in professions under automation pressure
- limiting forms of workplace surveillance and deskilling that hollow out responsibility
- ensuring that public institutions do not collapse into dashboard governance and ceremonial oversight

These are not anti-technology measures. They are pro-capability measures.

## The central principle

The question is not whether AI is good or bad. It is whether our institutions will use AI to make people more capable, or whether they will gradually redesign education, work, and public life so that fewer people are expected to exercise judgment and bear responsibility.

That distinction matters because freedom requires more than permission. It requires people still capable of using freedom well enough not to be dominated.

AI can help build a stronger society. But that will not happen automatically. It will depend on whether public institutions are designed to preserve the human capacities on which freedom, accountability, and democratic resilience depend.
